metadata.title: Barnett Bank of Marion Cty., NA v. Nelson, 517 U.S. 25 (1996) (No. 94-1837)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Barnett Bank of Marion Cty., NA v. Nelson

Opinion filed: 1996-03-26

Docket No.: 94-1837

Citations:
• 134 L. Ed. 2d 237
• 116 S. Ct. 1103
• 517 U.S. 25
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 2161

Case holding summaries:
• stating that grants of incidental powers to national banks normally preempt contrary state law
• “Did Congress, in enacting the Federal Statute, intend to exercise its constitutionally delegated authority to set aside the laws of a State? If so, the Supremacy Clause requires courts to follow federal, not state, law.”
• stating that grants of incidental powers to national banks normally preempt contrary state law
• "The word 'relates' is highly general, and this Court has interpreted it broadly in other pre-emption contexts."
• holding that a federal statute, 12 U.S.C. § 92, which expressly permits national banks to sell insurance in small towns, is a statute which "specifically relates to the business of insurance," and preempts a state statute which prohibits banks from selling insurance
• rejecting argument that Fabe 's "clear-statement" rule imposed any heightened requirement that a federal statute referring to "insurance" must also "use the words 'state law is pre-empted,' or the like"
• "The language of the Federal Statute before us is not general. It refers specifically to insurance. Its state regulatory implications are not surprising, nor do we believe them inadvertent."
• noting the parties' agreement that federal bankruptcy priority rules, although conflicting with state law, do not "specifically relate" to the business of insurance
• similar statement of Sen. Ferguson
• Federal Reserve Act provision that national banks "may continue . . . to receive . . . savings deposits" read as "declaratory of the right of a national bank to enter into or remain in that type of business"
• adopting the United States' view that language in the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 defining a "guaranteed benefit policy" as a certain kind of "insurance" policy "obviously and specifically relates to the business of insurance"
• federal regulation permitting, but not requiring, national banks to include in mortgage contracts a debt accelerating "due on sale" clause pre-empts a state law forbidding the use of such a clause
• enforcing 1864 amendments to National Bank Act expressly authorizing state taxation of national bank shares
• national banks' "power" to receive deposits pre-empts contrary state escheat law
• federal statute providing that local government units "may" expend federal funds for any governmental purpose pre-empts state law restricting their expenditure
• national banking system normally "independent, so far as powers conferred are concerned, of state legislation"
• state statute administering abandoned deposit accounts did not "unlawful[ly] encroac[h] on the rights and privileges of national banks"
• application to national banks of state statute forbidding certain real estate transfers by insolvent transferees would not "destro[y] or hampe[r]" national banks' functions
• interpreting similarly the words "`relating to' " in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978
• under McFadden Act, state branching restrictions apply to national banks
• "[W]here there exists a concurrent right of legislation in the States and in Congress, and the latter has exercised its power, there remains in the States no authority to legislate on the same matter"
• words "`relate to' " have "`broad common-sense meaning, such that a state law "relate[s] to" a benefit plan ". . . if it has a connection with or reference to such a plan"` "
• noting that "'[s]pecifically' can mean 'explicitly, particularly, [or] definitively'"
• Impossibility conflict would exist "if the federal law said, `you must sell insurance,' while the state law said, `you may not.'"
• holding that grants of powers to national banks "ordinarily preempt[] contrary state law" (citation and internal quotations omitted, emphasis added)
• referring three times to "ordinary English"
• "[U]sing ordinary English, one would say that this statute specifically relates to the 'business of insurance.' "
• conflict preemption applies where state law forbids conduct that federal law authorizes
• contrasting statute's use of the term "business activity," which may "implicitly refer . . . to insurance," with its use of the phrase "finance, banking, and insurance," which refers to insurance "specifically"
• setting forth definition of "specifically" and contrasting "specific" with "implicit"
• state statute could not bar small town national banks from selling insurance where federal statute gave the banks such authority
• conflict preemption applies to national banks
• holding that a federal statute permitting banks to act as agents of insurance companies, although not insurers themselves, was a statute regulating the "business of insurance" for McCarran-Ferguson purposes
• explaining that impossibility pre-emption arises "if the federal law said, `you must sell insurance,' while the state law said, `you may not'"
• "[The preemption] question is basically one of congressional intent"
• finding that federal law preempted Florida law which would have prohibited national banks from selling insurance
• recognizing the power of states to regulate national banks “where . . . doing so does not prevent or significantly interfere with the national 23 bank’s exercise of its powers”
• establishing preemption for state regulation of national banks
• noting that " '[s]pecifically' can mean 'explicitly, particularly, [or] definitively' "
• "Congress 'moved quickly,' enacting the McCarran-Ferguson Act 'to restore the supremacy of the States in the realm of insurance regulation.'"
• tracing the history of the McCarran-Ferguson Act
• interpreting the "specifically relates" language in the Act to refer to instances where "Congress had focused upon the insurance industry, and therefore, in all likelihood, consciously intended to exert upon the insurance industry whatever preemptive force accompanied its law"
• collecting examples of such 5 explicit statements
• noting that “subprime borrowers” need escrow 18 accounts for “budgeting assistance given their weaker credit histories”
• “Did Congress, in enacting the Federal Statute, intend to exercise its constitutionally delegated authority to set aside the laws of a State?”
• noting Congress sought to 11 “mitigat[e] . . . deceptive practices related to escrow accounts, mortgage servicing, 12 and appraisal practices”
• noting “approximately 50 percent 15 of all first lien subprime mortgages had escrows, compared to 71 percent of prime 16 loans”
• “[T]he escrow provisions . . . require[] 16 all subprime borrowers to have accounts established in conjunction with their 17 mortgages . . . .”
• "[T]he State Statute says, in essence, that banks cannot sell insurance in Florida except that an unaffiliated small town bank ( i.e., a bank that is not affiliated with a bank holding company) may sell insurance in a small town."
